P1.evidence: The strongest open in the batch. Application read back and converted into a hook rather than a recital: 'clearly, you're not someone who needs to be convinced that fitness matters, right? You do a lot. You swim, you do jujitsu, you lift, you hike... So you're doing everything right on paper, and yet something is still missing. Yeah. So let's figure it out together what exactly that is.' That names the prospect's actual problem in the first minute. The frame was an agenda rather than the four parts — 'could you brief me in on what's your situation right now? In terms of training, what do you do exactly? Then we go through the nutrition and the rest' — with nothing on what he needs. Agreement was implied by 'Sweet. Okay.' rather than asked for.

P2.evidence: Best baseline in the batch on the things that were asked. Training week captured in unusual detail and, crucially, the rep got the gap between intended and actual: 'Right now I'm honestly only averaging about twice a week with jujitsu.' Body fat asked for directly and the prospect pulled up a real InBody scan — 15% before keto, 11.8% on it. Sleep asked properly and followed up on tracking: 'And how do you sleep right now? What's your recovery?' then 'Do you track in any way your sleep quality? Like, do you have like a whoop band?' Diet covered in full including calorie counting, keto history and the guilty pleasure. Age was asked but not until 00:23:14, and height and weight never at all. Work was asserted from the application rather than asked. The critical failure is P2c: health conditions were never asked, only injuries, and the injury question was answered with 'Honestly, man, I'm pretty good' — so the disqualifying detail, a lower back that no longer tolerates barbell squats, did not surface until after the card had been charged.

P3.evidence: The surface goal was asked cleanly — 'what's the ultimate goal that you want to actually achieve? Like, what's the missing piece for you?' — and a concrete physical limitation surfaced through good follow-up on jiu-jitsu: gassing out after the third or fourth round. The bridge and the moving-better question both ran in one well-built move: 'When you think about what's becoming possible when you dial that in, actually, the fitness, the nutrition and everything, what becomes possible for you?' and it produced the deepest answer on the call — confidence, dominance at jiu-jitsu, and 'just feeling less lost in my fitness journey.' Then it stopped. Who-else-does-it-impact was never asked despite a girlfriend being mentioned twice. The rep responded to the best answer he got all call with 'that's actually golden' and immediately told a story about a different, almost-60 client, which moved the focus off the prospect. No reflect-back was ever attempted.

P4.evidence: Past attempts fully surfaced — keto, a previous coach, several programmes, years of Trevor's videos — and the rep asked the best question of the phase: 'I saw an application that you wrote, you've been following him for years, like, so what's held you back from contacting us sooner?' Outcomes were established with numbers, including that keto produced his best-ever result and he abandoned it anyway. Why it did not stick was volunteered rather than asked — 'I just couldn't stand eating bacon and cheese every day' — and the repeating success-then-failure pattern was named by the prospect, not diagnosed by the rep: 'I've tried a lot of different programs, I've had success, and then I've not had success, and I've kind of been on and off.' That admission was the doorway to P4f and it was not walked through.

P5.evidence: Nothing from this phase ran. No two-year question, no settle question, no why-not, no line in the sand. The rep did use a mild ageing frame — 'When I was 29, I could party, I could train, and I would still recover... after 30, and then when I hit 40, I noticed that recovery is not as fast' — but that was programme rationale for training less, not a cost of inaction. The consequence gap is the direct cause of what happened later: with no urgency banked, the first mention of competing holiday spend was met with a price cut rather than a challenge.

P6.evidence: The sloppiest commitment check in the batch, on the call that closed. The belief question was never asked. The all-in question was asked as a leading negative that made agreement the path of least resistance: 'I don't have to ask you, are you going to be fully committed when you sign up for this, right?' The recorded answer is the single word 'Nope' and the rep's reply is 'That's what I thought. Okay, next step is pretty easy, walk you through the investment.' Whatever the prospect actually meant, no genuine verbal yes was obtained before presenting, which is the entire point of the phase. This is exactly the kind of item that a good outcome must not be allowed to launder.

P11.evidence: By far the best execution of this phase in the batch. Payment link sent and card charged on the call, with confirmation: 'Oh, okay. I see it went through.' Trevor onboarding call booked live for Tuesday June 30th at 2.45pm Mountain and the confirmation read back by the prospect. The agreement email was chased when it did not arrive at first — 'Check my junk' — and located: 'You were invited to review and sign a document, this one?' — 'Yep.' But he was not walked through signing it on the call; the rep said 'That's it. That's it.' and moved on, so P11c is partial. Step four was covered properly: the onboarding form to complete before the Trevor call, and the Primal University Skool link with weekly live sessions.

objection_plays.detail: No think-about-it. He decided on the call.
A girlfriend is mentioned twice but never as a decision gate.

The stretch probe ran — 'is that something like a stretch for you right now?' — and produced the decisive answer: 'I have, I definitely have the money. It's more, it's just more than I thought it was going to be.' That is a value objection, not a capacity objection, and the correct response was to build value, not to move money around. Instead the rep produced the full payment-option menu, then cut the price. None of the financial picture ran, and when the prospect asked a direct question — 'Do you know what the interest rate is with Pava?' — he was answered with three monthly payment figures and never given a rate.

The single highest-value coaching point on the call. A clean OD trigger landed: 'The only thing is just the timing, because I got a trip to Europe coming up, and then I've got a jujitsu camp coming up, and those are both pretty expensive.' Not one OD move ran. 'Are you ever going to have another busy season?', 'things never slow down, when does it actually become the right time?', 'the longer you wait the harder this gets' were all directly applicable to a 29-year-old whose stated pattern is starting and stopping. The rep made small talk about Italy and Istanbul for thirty seconds and then said 'Tell you what? There's a three-month option... it's going to be 4K.' A scripted play was available, a $2,000 price cut was used instead, and the prospect accepted within four seconds.
No fear or doubt. He was pre-sold on Trevor after years of watching the content.

Script gap with a clinical edge. There is no post-close medical screen anywhere in the process, and this call demonstrates why one is needed: at 00:42:09, after the card had been charged and the onboarding call booked, the prospect volunteered 'CrossFit up my lower back pretty bad, so that's why I don't do CrossFit anymore. I can't squat, I can't do barbell squats anymore, actually, because of it.' The rep said 'Oh, damn' and the conversation moved to hiking. Nothing in the process obliges anyone to revisit a material physical limitation disclosed after payment, and nothing routed it to Trevor before the onboarding call.

notes: A closed deal that scores poorly on process and should be read as a warning rather than a model. Baseline and P11 were genuinely excellent — sleep, energy, body fat, planned-versus-actual training days, then payment, onboarding call, agreement chase and Skool link all executed. Everything in between leaked: no health conditions question, no consequence frame, a leading commitment check answered with one ambiguous word, and a clean timing objection answered with a $2,000 discount to a man who had just said he had the money. Coach: when a prospect says 'I definitely have the money, it's just more than I thought', the objection is value and the price must not move; and add a health-conditions question that is separate from the injuries question, because 'Honestly, man, I'm pretty good' concealed a back that cannot tolerate a barbell squat.
